title: The association between epilepsy and inflammatory bowel disease in adults: Findings from the 2023 National Health Interview Survey
content:
by Xianming Su, Yueying Lin, Shuyan Shen, Liya An, Ting Yang, Yuxing Qi, Xingzong Huang, Yinlong Deng, Jian Hu, Haiyu He, Dali Sun

Background

Evidence suggests a bidirectional association between nervous system diseases and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but the association between epilepsy and IBD in adults remains unexplored. This study examined the adult epilepsy–IBD association using data from the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).

Methods

Adult participants from the 2023 NHIS were selected based on inclusion and exclusion criteria. Baseline characteristics were compared using weighted analyses. Weighted multivariable logistic regression models with progressive covariate adjustment were performed to evaluate the association between epilepsy and IBD. Sensitivity analyses included a parsimonious model and Firth penalized likelihood logistic regression. Subgroup analyses stratified by age and sex were also conducted, and the unadjusted association was additionally examined in the 2015–2016 data.

Results

Among 27,127 adults analyzed, 532 had IBD, including 26 with both epilepsy and IBD. In baseline comparisons, individuals with epilepsy had a significantly higher prevalence of IBD (p < 0.001). In weighted logistic regression, epilepsy was positively associated with IBD. The association persisted in the fully adjusted model (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.04–2.45, p = 0.025) and the parsimonious model (OR 2.74, 95% CI 1.82–4.13, p < 0.001). Firth regression yielded results in the same direction. Larger point estimates were observed in adults aged 30–39 years (OR 5.19, 95% CI 1.96–11.46) and males (OR 3.04, 95% CI 1.54–5.40), although interaction tests were not significant (age: p = 0.619; sex: p = 0.586). A positive unadjusted association was also observed in 2015–2016 data (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.37–3.05).

Conclusions

The prevalence of IBD was higher among US adults with epilepsy than among those without epilepsy. These findings provide preliminary evidence from a nationally representative population for a potential epilepsy–IBD association and suggest that this comorbidity pattern warrants further attention in clinical and epidemiological research.
